interactions.summary: Students test several explanations for Lucifer's fall, including his identity as angel of light, God's favored lieutenant, and a possible exceptional status near free will, while Jiang keeps returning to the unresolved contradiction that angels supposedly lack free will.

claims.claim: A student suggests Lucifer's closeness to light may paradoxically expose him to darkness, making him the most likely angel to turn.
Students describe Lucifer as God's most loved lieutenant or chief servant, which intensifies the puzzle of why such a being would fail.

Jiang tentatively allows that Lucifer may have been a head servant with enough free will to screw up, but the class immediately objects that this would contradict the premise that angels lack free will and even consciousness.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture speculation and class pushback dated 2026-06-24.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang briefly tries the simplest humanizing answer, that Lucifer just had enough agency to screw up, only for the class's own premises to block it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he had free will. He screwed up
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows the discussion tightening around a contradiction that easy moral psychology cannot solve.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The class's term for Lucifer as God's chief subordinate or head servant within the cosmic hierarchy.

chronology_notes.note: The machine metaphor gives way here to rank and hierarchy questions: the class now treats Lucifer's fall as a structural puzzle about angelic status, favor, and whether any nonhuman being can deviate at all.

uncertainty_notes.note: This packet is dominated by open class speculation rather than settled doctrine; Jiang does not endorse a final account of angelic agency here.
